title: Stacks, Queues, Deques, and Heaps
summary: Use ArrayDeque as a stack, a queue, and a double-ended deque, and PriorityQueue as a min-heap or max-heap.
intro: Many problems only ever need the newest item, the oldest item, or the smallest item. `ArrayDeque` gives you the first two from either end, and `PriorityQueue` gives you the third, each in fast constant or logarithmic time.

steps.title: ArrayDeque as a stack
steps.body:
A stack is last in, first out: the item you added most recently comes off first. Use it for undo, matching brackets, and anything you must finish in reverse order. In Java, declare it as a `Deque` and build an `ArrayDeque`:

```java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

Deque<Character> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
stack.push('(');                      // add on top
stack.push('[');
System.out.println(stack.peek());     // [ (look, do not remove)
System.out.println(stack.pop());      // [ (remove the top)
System.out.println(stack.size());     // 1
System.out.println(stack.isEmpty());  // false
```

Gotcha: `pop()` on an empty stack throws `NoSuchElementException`, so check `isEmpty()` first whenever the stack might be empty. `peek()` on an empty stack returns `null` instead.

`System.out.println(stack)` prints the elements top first, so after pushing 1, 2, 3 you see `[3, 2, 1]`.

Prefer `ArrayDeque` over the old `Stack` class: `Stack` is slower and prints bottom first.

example.title: Bracket checker
example.prompt: Check three bracket strings for balance with a stack, then push and pop numbers and print the stack.
example.output:
{[()]} balanced: true
([)] balanced: false
()) balanced: false
Popped: 3
Stack: [2, 1]
Top: 2
Size: 2
example.explanation: Each opening bracket is pushed, and each closing bracket pops the most recent opener, which must match it. In `([)]` the `)` pops `[`, so it fails. In `())` the last `)` finds the stack empty, and the `isEmpty()` check returns `false` instead of letting `pop()` throw. A string is balanced only if the stack ends empty. The number stack pops 3, the last value pushed, and prints the rest top first as `[2, 1]`. The pop is stored in `popped` before printing, so nothing is changed inside a print statement.

practice.title: Undo history
practice.prompt:
Undo the last two edits in an editor's history stack.

1. Push every word of `edits` onto `history`, in array order.
2. Undo twice: each time, if `history` is not empty, pop the top and print `Undo: ` and the word.
3. On three lines, print `History: ` and the stack, `Top: ` and `peek()`, and `Size: ` and `size()`.

Expected output:

```text
Undo: footer
Undo: typo
History: [chart, intro, title]
Top: chart
Size: 3
```

tests.output:
Undo: footer
Undo: typo
History: [chart, intro, title]
Top: chart
Size: 3

hints: `push` puts each word on top, so `footer`, the last word pushed, is the first one popped.
Repeat the undo with a loop that runs twice. Check `isEmpty()` before each `pop()`, and store the popped word in a variable before you print it.

steps.title: ArrayDeque as a queue
steps.body:
A queue is first in, first out: items leave in the order they arrived, like a line at a shop. Declare it as a `Queue` and build an `ArrayDeque`:

```java
import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Queue;

Queue<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
queue.offer("Ana");                // add at the back
queue.offer("Ben");
System.out.println(queue.peek());  // Ana (look at the front)
System.out.println(queue.poll());  // Ana (remove the front)
System.out.println(queue.size());  // 1
```

Unlike a stack's `pop()`, which throws on an empty stack, `poll()` and `peek()` never throw. On an empty queue they return `null`, so you can drain a queue with `while (!queue.isEmpty())` and call `poll()` inside.

Gotcha: `ArrayDeque` does not accept `null` elements. `offer(null)` throws `NullPointerException`, which is what keeps that `null` from `poll()` unambiguous: it always means empty.

`ArrayDeque` is faster than `LinkedList` as a queue, and much faster than `list.remove(0)`, which shifts every element.

example.title: Shop line
example.prompt: Serve customers in arrival order, with one late arrival joining the back of the line.
example.output:
Served Ana
Waiting: 3
Next: Ben
Served Ben
Served Cara
Served Dev
Next: null
example.explanation: `offer` adds each customer at the back, and `poll` takes Ana from the front because she arrived first. Dev arrives late, so he joins behind Cara. The `while` loop polls until the queue is empty, serving everyone in arrival order. The last `peek()` finds nothing and returns `null` instead of throwing.

practice.title: Printer queue
practice.prompt:
Simulate a printer queue that prints jobs in the order they were sent.

1. Offer the five jobs in `jobs` to `printer`, in array order.
2. Poll two jobs and print `Printing ` and each job name.
3. Offer `invoice.pdf`, then print `Waiting: ` and the size on one line and `Next: ` and `peek()` on the next.
4. Poll the rest in a loop, printing `Printing ` and each name.
5. Print `Next: ` and `peek()` once more.

Expected output:

```text
Printing report.pdf
Printing photo.png
Waiting: 4
Next: slides.ppt
Printing slides.ppt
Printing memo.txt
Printing chart.png
Printing invoice.pdf
Next: null
```

tests.output:
Printing report.pdf
Printing photo.png
Waiting: 4
Next: slides.ppt
Printing slides.ppt
Printing memo.txt
Printing chart.png
Printing invoice.pdf
Next: null

hints: `offer` adds at the back and `poll` removes from the front.
Drain the rest with `while (!printer.isEmpty())` and call `poll()` inside the loop.

steps.title: Both ends of a Deque
steps.body:
A `Deque` (double-ended queue, said "deck") adds and removes at both ends. Each end has its own methods:

```java
Deque<Integer> d = new ArrayDeque<>();
d.offerLast(20);                    // add at the back
d.offerFirst(10);                   // add at the front
System.out.println(d);              // [10, 20]
System.out.println(d.peekFirst());  // 10
System.out.println(d.peekLast());   // 20
System.out.println(d.pollFirst());  // 10, leaves [20]
System.out.println(d.pollLast());   // 20, leaves []
```

Like a queue's `poll` and `peek`, these return `null` on an empty deque instead of throwing.

The stack methods are the same front end: `push` adds at the front like `offerFirst`, and `pop` removes the front like `pollFirst`, except `pop` throws on an empty deque. That is why a stack prints top first. A queue's `offer` and `poll` are `offerLast` and `pollFirst`.

Gotcha: a `Deque<Character>` holds `Character` objects, so `d.pollFirst() != d.pollLast()` compares references. It happens to work for plain ASCII letters, because Java reuses cached `Character` objects below 128, but it breaks for a letter like `é`. Store each one in a `char` first, then compare the values with `!=`.

example.title: Two ended numbers
example.prompt: Build a deque from both ends, then check two words for palindromes by polling from both ends.
example.output:
Deque: [5, 10, 20, 30]
First: 5
Last: 30
After push: [1, 5, 10, 20, 30]
racecar: true
stack: false
example.explanation: `offerLast` appends 20 and 30, then each `offerFirst` puts its value in front, so 5 ends up first. `push(1)` lands at the same front end. The palindrome check loads every letter at the back, then repeatedly takes one letter from each end. Storing them in `char` variables unboxes them, so `!=` compares letters. When one or zero letters remain, every pair matched.

practice.title: Urgent tasks
practice.prompt:
Keep a task deque with urgent work at the front, then check two phrases for palindromes ignoring spaces and case.

1. Add `email` with `offerLast`, `server down` with `offerFirst`, `lunch order` with `offerLast`, and `fire alarm` with `offerFirst`.
2. Print `Tasks: ` and the deque, `First: ` and `peekFirst()`, and `Last: ` and `peekLast()`.
3. In `isPalindrome`, add each character that is not whitespace to the back of a `Deque<Character>`, lowercased with `Character.toLowerCase`.
4. Compare `pollFirst()` with `pollLast()` while more than one character remains.
5. For each phrase, print the phrase, `: `, and the result.

Expected output:

```text
Tasks: [fire alarm, server down, email, lunch order]
First: fire alarm
Last: lunch order
Never odd or even: true
Open the door: false
```

tests.output:
Tasks: [fire alarm, server down, email, lunch order]
First: fire alarm
Last: lunch order
Never odd or even: true
Open the door: false

hints: `offerFirst` puts a task in front of everything already there.
Skip a character with `Character.isWhitespace(c)`, and add `Character.toLowerCase(c)` with `offerLast`.
Store `pollFirst()` and `pollLast()` in `char` variables before comparing them.

steps.title: PriorityQueue

example.title: Heaps and tasks
example.prompt: Sort numbers with a min-heap, take the three largest from a max-heap, and poll tasks by priority with ties broken by id.
example.output:
Heap order: [1, 2, 8, 5, 3]
Smallest: 1
Sorted: 1 2 3 5 8
Large: 8
Large: 5
Large: 3
Tasks: 5
Task 7 priority 1
Task 2 priority 2
Task 4 priority 2
Task 1 priority 3
Task 5 priority 3
example.explanation: The printed heap `[1, 2, 8, 5, 3]` only promises that the smallest value is first, while polling in a loop yields `1 2 3 5 8`. `Collections.reverseOrder()` flips the heap, so three polls return the three largest values. The task comparator orders by priority, the second slot. Tasks 4 and 2 tie on priority 2, so the tie-breaker compares ids and task 2 comes out first. Each polled `int[]` is printed with `t[0]` and `t[1]`.

practice.title: Triage queue
practice.prompt:
Call patients from a triage queue, highest urgency first.

1. Create `queue` as a `PriorityQueue<int[]>` whose comparator puts higher urgency (slot 1) first and breaks ties by lower id (slot 0).
2. Offer every `int[]{id, urgency}` from `patients`.
3. Print `Waiting: ` and the size, then `Next: ` and the id of the patient `peek()` returns.
4. Poll every patient and print `Patient `, the id, ` urgency `, and the urgency.

Expected output:

```text
Waiting: 6
Next: 2
Patient 2 urgency 9
Patient 5 urgency 9
Patient 4 urgency 7
Patient 1 urgency 5
Patient 3 urgency 5
Patient 6 urgency 2
```

tests.output:
Waiting: 6
Next: 2
Patient 2 urgency 9
Patient 5 urgency 9
Patient 4 urgency 7
Patient 1 urgency 5
Patient 3 urgency 5
Patient 6 urgency 2

hints: Start from the task comparator in the example. Only the urgency comparison changes.
`Integer.compare(x, y)` puts smaller values first. Swap its two arguments to put larger values first, and keep the id tie-breaker as it is.

recap:
- Declare a stack as `Deque<T> stack = new ArrayDeque<>()` and use `push`, `pop`, `peek`, `isEmpty()`, and `size()`. It is last in, first out.
- `pop()` on an empty deque throws `NoSuchElementException`, so check `isEmpty()` first. `println(stack)` lists the top first.
- Declare a queue as `Queue<T> queue = new ArrayDeque<>()` and use `offer` (back) and `poll` (front). It is first in, first out.
- `poll()` and `peek()` return `null` when empty, and `ArrayDeque` rejects `null` elements.
- A `Deque` works at both ends with `offerFirst`, `offerLast`, `pollFirst`, `pollLast`, `peekFirst`, and `peekLast`. `push` and `pop` use the front.
- `PriorityQueue` is a min-heap. Use `Collections.reverseOrder()` for a max-heap, or a comparator lambda with `Integer.compare` and a tie-breaker for `int[]` entries.
- A heap prints in heap order. Poll in a loop to get sorted output.
